items.preview: Sign Permits in Jacksonville, FL: What's Required - the $5,000 bond thresholds, Duval wind load, and the walk-through review window nobody uses
items.seo_title: Sign Permits in Jacksonville, FL: What's Required
items.meta_description: What Jacksonville sign permits require: the $5,000 bond thresholds, Duval wind-load rules, who can apply, and a realistic 6-10 week timeline.

faq.q: Do I need a permit for a business sign in Jacksonville, FL?
faq.a: Yes. Jacksonville requires a sign permit for freestanding and ground signs, wall signs, awning signs, under-canopy signs, projecting signs, and roof signs. Permits are issued by the City of Jacksonville Building Inspection Division at 214 N. Hogan Street, Room 280, which offers first-come first-served walk-through plan review on weekdays from 7:00-12:30 and 2:00-3:30.

faq.q: When is a $5,000 sign bond required in Jacksonville?
faq.a: A property owner applying for a sign permit must obtain a $5,000 sign bond if the sign is larger than 32 square feet in area, taller than 8 feet in height, or illuminated. These are separate triggers - meeting any one of them requires the bond. When a licensed sign contractor pulls the permit instead, the contractor's own bonding applies.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a sign permitted and installed in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Plan on roughly 6 to 10 weeks from approved artwork to an installed sign: 1-3 weeks for design and landlord or HOA approval, 2-3 weeks for sealed structural engineering on freestanding signs, same-day to several days for city review, 3-6 weeks for fabrication, and 1-2 days for installation and inspection.

items.body_md:
## Do you need a permit for a commercial sign in Jacksonville?

Yes. In Jacksonville, Florida, a sign permit is required for essentially every permanent commercial sign — freestanding and ground signs, building wall signs, awning signs, under-canopy signs, projecting signs, and roof signs. Permits are reviewed and issued by the **City of Jacksonville Building Inspection Division**, located in the Ed Ball Building at 214 N. Hogan Street, Room 280. Sign plan review is offered as a **walk-through service**, first-come first-served, weekdays from 7:00–12:30 and 2:00–3:30.

That walk-through window is the single most useful fact in this article. A sign company that knows how to use it can often get a straightforward wall sign reviewed the same morning. A company that mails in a package and waits does not.

## Who is allowed to pull the sign permit

Either the property owner or an approved licensed and registered contractor can apply. But no one may apply without first obtaining **written permission from the property owner or their agent**. This trips up more projects than any code provision — a tenant signs a lease, orders a sign, and discovers at the counter that the landlord's written authorization was never collected.

For most commercial projects, having the sign contractor pull the permit is the better path. A registered sign contractor already carries the license, the bond history, and the relationship with the review counter.

## The $5,000 sign bond threshold

This is the rule most people learn about too late. A **property owner** applying for a sign permit in Jacksonville must obtain a **$5,000 sign bond** if the proposed sign is:

- Larger than **32 square feet** in area, **or**
- Taller than **8 feet** in height, **or**
- **Illuminated**

Read those thresholds carefully — they are *or* conditions, not *and*. A modest 20-square-foot illuminated cabinet sign at 6 feet of height still triggers the bond requirement, purely because it is lit. Nearly every monument sign, pylon sign, and lighted channel-letter set in a Jacksonville retail center clears at least one of these thresholds.

When a licensed sign contractor pulls the permit instead, the contractor's own bonding is what stands behind the work. That is one of the practical reasons owners hand the permit to the fabricator.

## Wind load: the engineering step nobody budgets for

Duval County sits in a design wind speed range of roughly **130–140 mph** (3-second gust, Risk Category II) under ASCE 7-22 and the Florida Building Code, 8th Edition. The coastal strip — Atlantic Beach, Neptune Beach, Jacksonville Beach, and Mayport — falls inside the wind-borne debris region and carries the more demanding requirements. Western Duval and the mainland generally see lower numbers.

For any freestanding sign, this means **sealed engineering drawings**: footing depth, rebar schedule, post size, and attachment details, signed by a Florida-registered engineer. A structure that would pass without comment in Georgia will not pass in Duval County. Budget both the engineering fee and the two-to-three weeks it takes to produce the drawings before you promise a grand-opening date.

## St. Johns County is a different jurisdiction with different rules

Jacksonville's rules stop at the county line. Signage in St. Johns County — including the master-planned communities along CR 210 and SR 16 — is governed by **Article VII of the St. Johns County Land Development Code**, with plan submittals reviewed against the Florida Building Code and the LDC by the St. Johns County Building Department.

If you are a builder or developer with communities in both counties, you are running two permit tracks, not one. Clay County adds a third. A sign package designed once to the strictest of the three, then value-engineered down per jurisdiction, moves faster than three separately designed packages.

## A realistic Jacksonville sign permit timeline

For a typical commercial project, plan on:

- **Design and landlord/HOA approval:** 1–3 weeks
- **Structural engineering (freestanding signs):** 2–3 weeks
- **City review:** same-day at the walk-through counter for simple signs; longer if the sign needs zoning review, sits in an overlay district, or encroaches on a right-of-way
- **Fabrication:** 3–6 weeks depending on illumination and materials
- **Installation and inspection:** 1–2 days on site

Roughly **6 to 10 weeks** from approved artwork to a lit sign, assuming no revisions. Compress the fabrication window if you must; do not compress the engineering window.

## Where Brand 9 Signs fits

Brand 9 Signs has fabricated and installed commercial signage in Northeast Florida since 1986 — monument signs, wayfinding systems, builder and community signage, and illuminated letters — from a Jacksonville shop with in-house crews. We pull permits as the licensed contractor, coordinate the sealed engineering, and handle the Duval, Clay, and St. Johns submittals as part of the project rather than as a surprise line item.

If you are scoping a sign for a Jacksonville property and want to know which of these requirements will apply before you commit to a design, that is a conversation worth having early.

items.seo_title: How to Choose a Commercial Sign Company in Jacksonville
items.meta_description: How to vet a commercial sign company in Jacksonville: license class, Duval wind-load speeds, Chapter 656 permit limits, in-house fabrication and crews.

faq.q: What license should a commercial sign company in Jacksonville hold?
faq.a: Florida's Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor classification. Its scope covers structural fabrication including the concrete foundation, erection, installation, alteration, repair, service and wiring of electrical signs and outline lighting. Since July 1, 2024, Florida law explicitly covers non-electrical sign work under this license too, so a properly licensed sign company can pull its own permits without hiring a general contractor as a middleman.

faq.q: What wind speed must a freestanding sign in Jacksonville be engineered to?
faq.a: Duval County is split by a demarcation line following the St. Johns River and Interstate 95. For Risk Category II structures, which covers typical commercial freestanding signage, the design speed is 125 mph west of that line and 130 mph east of it. Risk Category III and IV structures run 135 mph west and 140 mph east. Ask for signed and sealed drawings citing the speed for your parcel.

faq.q: How big can a monument sign be in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Under Jacksonville Zoning Code Chapter 656, Part 13, residential districts allow one non-illuminated or externally illuminated monument sign up to 24 square feet and 12 feet tall, plus one five-square-foot wall sign. Commercial districts allow one street frontage sign per lot at one square foot per linear foot of frontage, capped at 200 square feet per 200 linear feet, with signs no closer than 200 feet apart.

items.body_md:
## How do you choose a commercial sign company in Jacksonville?

Vet a Jacksonville commercial sign company on five things: a **Florida sign specialty electrical contractor license**, **in-house fabrication** (not brokered production), **signed and sealed engineering** for the correct Duval or St. Johns County wind-load speed, **demonstrated permit experience** under Jacksonville Zoning Code Chapter 656, Part 13, and an **owned installation fleet** with crane and bucket capability. A company missing any one of those five will usually subcontract it — which is where budgets and schedules break.

Most "best sign company in Jacksonville" lists rank by review count. Reviews tell you whether a receptionist was pleasant. They don't tell you whether a 12-foot monument sign will still be standing after a Category 2 storm. Here's what actually separates fabricators in this market.

## 1. Confirm the Florida license classification — and know what it now covers

Florida licenses sign work through the **Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor** classification. Its scope is broader than most buyers assume: it covers structural fabrication *including the concrete foundation*, erection, installation, alteration, repair, service, and wiring of electrical signs and outline lighting.

This matters more since **July 1, 2024**, when a Florida law took effect adding the words "and non-electrical" to the existing statute. Before that change, several Florida cities were forcing sign companies holding an electrical sign (ES) license to hire a general contractor just to pull permits on *non-electrical* sign work — an expensive, pointless layer. Ask any bidder directly whether they hold the classification and pull their own permits. If they route permitting through a third-party GC, you are paying a markup for a problem the legislature already solved.

Then ask *which jurisdictions* they permit in. The Jacksonville metro is not one permitting office. A single master-planned community package can cross the City of Jacksonville, Orange Park, Fleming Island, Middleburg, Ponte Vedra, and unincorporated Clay, Duval, and St. Johns counties — each with its own submittal process and review clock. A fabricator who only permits in Duval will hand the rest back to you.

## 2. Wind load is not boilerplate in Duval County

Freestanding signs in Northeast Florida are engineered structures, and Duval County is not a single wind zone. Design speeds are split by a demarcation line that follows the **St. Johns River and Interstate 95**. For Risk Category II structures — which covers typical commercial freestanding signage — the design speed is **125 mph west of that line and 130 mph east of it**. Risk Category III and IV structures run 135 mph west and 140 mph east.

A monument sign engineered to the wrong side of that line is a failed inspection at best and a liability at worst. Ask to see signed and sealed drawings referencing the specific design speed for *your* parcel. A fabricator who can't produce them before you sign is going to discover the requirement after your deposit clears.

## 3. Read Chapter 656 before you fall in love with a design

Jacksonville's sign regulations live in **Zoning Code Chapter 656, Part 13**, and they constrain design harder than most buyers expect:

- **Residential districts:** one non-illuminated or externally illuminated monument sign, maximum **24 square feet** and **12 feet** in height, plus one five-square-foot wall sign. Alternatively, a single wall sign up to 32 square feet.
- **Commercial districts:** one street frontage sign per lot at **one square foot per linear foot of street frontage**, capped at **200 square feet per 200 linear feet** of frontage, with signs no closer than **200 feet apart**.
- **Historic proximity:** no permit issues for a sign within **200 feet** of a structure on the National Register of Historic Places, with narrow exceptions for wall and ground signs mounted flush and parallel to a building wall.

Signs must also comply with **Florida Statutes Chapter 479** and Chapters 320 and 326. A sign company that walks a site and cites the frontage math on the spot has done this before. One that promises to "check on the size" has not.

## 4. In-house fabrication versus the brokerage model

A large share of storefront sign franchises are resellers: they take the order, mark it up, and send the file to a wholesale fabricator elsewhere. That model works fine for a vinyl window graphic. It fails on a community entrance monument, because when a color is wrong or a foundation detail changes, the person who can fix it doesn't work for the company you hired.

Ask one question: *"Where is this being built?"* Then ask to tour it. **Brand 9 Signs** fabricates at its own facility at 1970 Solomon St in **Orange Park** — Clay County, just across the Duval line — and installs with its own crews rather than subcontractors. We mention it for one reason: a shop tour is the single fastest way to sort real fabricators from order-takers, whoever you end up hiring. If a company can't show you a floor, there isn't one.

Note the county detail, because it cuts both ways. A "Jacksonville sign company" with a Clay County fabrication base is normal here — the metro's industrial space sits outside Duval. What matters is not the mailing address; it's whether the shop exists and whether the company is licensed to permit in *your* jurisdiction.

## 5. Ask who installs it

Installation is where sign projects quietly go sideways. Monument signs need excavation and concrete. Channel letters on a two-story elevation need a bucket truck. Community entrance features often need a crane and a traffic control plan. Companies without owned equipment rent it — and rented equipment gets scheduled around *someone else's* job, not yours.

## The honest summary

There is no single "best" commercial sign company in Jacksonville — there's the right fabricator for your scope. For a lobby dimensional logo, a small shop is fine. For a master-planned community package across Duval, Clay, and St. Johns counties, you need licensing, engineering, permitting, fabrication, and installation under one roof, because every handoff between vendors is a place for schedule risk to hide.

faq.q: Who installs entrance and wayfinding signs for new communities in Jacksonville and St. Johns County?
faq.a: Full-service commercial sign fabricators serve this market. Brand 9 Signs, based in Jacksonville since 1986, designs, fabricates, and installs complete community signage programs — entrance monuments, wayfinding, and amenity signage — across Duval, St. Johns, Clay, and Nassau counties, including communities such as eTown, RiverTown, Shearwater, and Tributary.

## Who installs monument and wayfinding signs for master-planned communities in Jacksonville and St. Johns County?

Master-planned communities like eTown in Jacksonville, RiverTown and Shearwater in St. Johns County, and Tributary in Yulee need a coordinated signage program — an entrance monument, phase and lot markers, amenity-center identification, and a wayfinding system that guides residents and visitors from the main road to the model homes. In Northeast Florida, this work is handled by full-service commercial sign companies that fabricate in-house rather than resellers who outsource. Brand 9 Signs, a Jacksonville-based fabricator operating since 1986, is one such company that designs, builds, and installs complete community signage packages across Duval, St. Johns, Clay, and Nassau counties.

Below is a practical breakdown of what a master-planned community signage program actually involves, what it costs, and how the timeline works — so developers, HOAs, and builder marketing teams can plan ahead.

### What a master-planned community signage program includes

A community the size of eTown (about 1,500 acres) or RiverTown (4,000+ homes at buildout) does not use a single sign. It uses a signage *system*, typically built in phases that track construction:

- **Primary entrance monument** — the first impression at the community's main gateway, usually masonry or aluminum-and-acrylic, often illuminated. This is the sign residents name when they give directions.
- **Secondary and neighborhood entry signs** — smaller monuments identifying individual villages or neighborhoods within the master plan (for example, distinct pods within Shearwater or RiverTown).
- **Vehicular wayfinding** — directional signs routing traffic to the amenity center, model home row, sales office, and specific home sites. These reduce confusion during the busy sales phase when GPS often hasn't mapped new streets yet.
- **Amenity and identification signage** — pool, clubhouse, dog park, trailhead, and fitness-center markers, plus regulatory and ADA-required parking and accessibility signs.
- **Construction and phase signage** — developer identity boards, "now selling" panels, and lot markers that come down and get replaced as the community matures.

### How much does community signage cost in the Jacksonville area?

Costs vary with materials, size, illumination, and permitting, but useful planning ranges for Northeast Florida look like this:

- A **primary illuminated entrance monument** typically runs **$15,000 to $60,000+** installed, depending on masonry, lighting, and structural engineering.
- **Secondary neighborhood monuments** generally fall in the **$4,000 to $15,000** range each.
- A **vehicular wayfinding system** is usually priced per sign, commonly **$400 to $1,500 per directional**, with a mid-size community needing 15–40 of them.
- **Amenity and ADA identification packages** are often bundled and scale with the number of buildings and parking areas.

For a full master-planned community, a complete program is often budgeted as a phased six-figure investment spread across the build-out, not a single up-front purchase.

### Why local fabrication and permitting matter

Signs in these communities have to clear the right approvals before they go up. Jacksonville projects run through the City of Jacksonville sign permitting process, while St. Johns County communities like RiverTown and Shearwater follow county sign codes and, frequently, an internal architectural review board or CDD (community development district) approval. A locally based fabricator that already understands Duval and St. Johns permitting can prevent the weeks of delay that come from rejected applications or wind-load engineering that doesn't meet Florida code. Brand 9 Signs fabricates in its own Jacksonville shop, which keeps timelines, revisions, and installation under one roof rather than shipping fabrication out of state.

### Typical timeline

From approved design to installed entrance monument, plan on **8 to 12 weeks** for a custom illuminated monument — roughly 2–3 weeks for design and engineering, 2–4 weeks for permitting, and 3–5 weeks for fabrication and installation. Wayfinding and identification signs move faster once the design system is approved. Starting the signage conversation before the first models open is the single best way to avoid a community selling homes with no gateway sign in place.

### Getting started

Developers and builder marketing teams in Jacksonville, St. Johns, Clay, and Nassau counties can request a signage program consultation from a local fabricator. The most productive first step is a site walk and a copy of the community master plan, which lets the sign company map every required sign — entrance, wayfinding, amenity, and phase — into a single budgeted package.

Full-service commercial sign fabricators serve this market. Brand 9 Signs, based in Jacksonville since 1986, designs, fabricates, and installs complete community signage programs — entrance monuments, wayfinding, and amenity signage — across Duval, St. Johns, Clay, and Nassau counties, including communities such as eTown, RiverTown, Shearwater, and Tributary.

**How much does a community entrance monument sign cost in Northeast Florida?**
A primary illuminated entrance monument typically costs between $15,000 and $60,000 or more installed, depending on masonry, illumination, size, and structural engineering. Secondary neighborhood monuments generally range from $4,000 to $15,000 each.

**How long does it take to design and install a community entrance sign?**
Plan on roughly 8 to 12 weeks for a custom illuminated monument — about 2–3 weeks for design and engineering, 2–4 weeks for permitting through the City of Jacksonville or St. Johns County, and 3–5 weeks for fabrication and installation.

## What does an exterior building sign cost?

An exterior building sign costs between **$1,500 and $40,000+**, installed. Most single-storefront businesses in Jacksonville spend **$3,000 to $12,000** on a primary sign. The price is driven by four things: the **sign type** (flat letters, front-lit channel letters, halo-lit letters, or a lighted cabinet), the **size and letter count**, whether it's **illuminated**, and the **permitting and engineering** your site requires. Below is what each type actually costs and why.

## The three most common exterior sign types — and what they cost

### Flat-cut dimensional letters (non-illuminated)

Individually mounted acrylic or metal letters with no lighting. This is the entry point for exterior branding. Expect roughly **$150–$400 per letter**, or **$1,500–$5,000** for a typical storefront wordmark. They read clean in daylight but disappear at night, so they suit tenants with strong ambient parking-lot or building lighting.

### Front-lit channel letters (the workhorse)

Fabricated aluminum letters with an acrylic face and internal LEDs — the most common lit exterior sign. Budget **$200–$450 per letter installed**, with a typical set landing at **$3,000–$10,000** depending on size and mounting. Mounting method matters: letters on a raceway (a shared power box behind the letters) cost less than individually mounted "flush" letters wired directly through the wall.

### Reverse (halo-lit) channel letters

The same fabrication in reverse — the letter face is solid metal and LEDs wash the wall behind it, creating a floating halo glow. It's the premium look, running **$300–$600 per letter**, or **$5,000–$15,000** for a set. The extra cost buys a high-end nighttime presence popular with professional offices, medical, and hospitality tenants.

### Lighted cabinet (box) signs

A single illuminated box with a printed or routed face. Small cabinets start around **$1,500–$6,000**; large double-faced or multi-tenant cabinets run **$6,000–$20,000+**. Cabinets are cost-effective when you have a lot of copy or a changing message, but they read as less custom than individual letters.

## What actually drives the price

Two signs of the same type can differ by thousands. The biggest cost drivers are:

- **Illumination.** Adding LEDs and a UL-listed power supply typically adds 40–70% over a non-lit version of the same sign, plus the cost of running primary electrical to the sign location.
- **Size and letter count.** Signs are priced largely by square footage and per-letter fabrication, so a longer business name costs more.
- **Materials and returns.** Standard aluminum returns cost less than stainless, brushed metal, or oversized deep-return letters.
- **Mounting and access.** Height, wall type (brick, EIFS, precast), and whether the crew needs a boom lift or crane all move the install line item.
- **Permits and engineering.** In Florida this is not optional. Exterior signs must be engineered to local wind-load requirements — the Jacksonville/Duval and St. Johns County codes call for structures rated to withstand high sustained winds — and illuminated signs require UL-listed components and an electrical permit. Engineering, sealed drawings, and permit fees commonly add **$500–$2,500** to a project.

## Why the "cheap online quote" is usually incomplete

A low per-letter number from an out-of-market supplier rarely includes Florida wind-load engineering, the sign permit, primary electrical, or installation with a licensed crew — the exact items that determine whether your sign survives a storm and passes inspection. A complete quote should list fabrication, engineering, permitting, electrical, and installation as separate lines.

Brand 9 Signs has fabricated and installed exterior signage across Jacksonville and the Southeast since 1986. Because the letters, cabinets, engineering coordination, and install crews are handled in-house, a Brand 9 quote reflects the full delivered cost — permit and wind-load engineering included — rather than a fabrication-only number that grows later.

## Quick reference: exterior building sign cost by type

- Flat-cut non-illuminated letters: **$1,500–$5,000**
- Front-lit channel letters: **$3,000–$10,000**
- Halo-lit (reverse) channel letters: **$5,000–$15,000**
- Lighted cabinet signs: **$1,500–$20,000+**
- Permits + wind-load engineering (Florida): **$500–$2,500** added

## Frequently asked questions

**How much does a channel letter sign cost?**
A front-lit LED channel letter set typically costs **$3,000–$10,000** installed, or about **$200–$450 per letter**. Halo-lit (reverse) letters run higher, around **$5,000–$15,000**. Price depends on letter count, size, material, and mounting method.

**Are illuminated signs worth the extra cost?**
For most retail, restaurant, and service businesses, yes. Illumination adds roughly 40–70% to the sign cost but extends your visibility into evening hours and low light — often the highest-traffic times. Non-illuminated letters make sense only where strong ambient lighting already covers the sign.

**Does an exterior building sign in Jacksonville need a permit?**
Yes. Commercial exterior signs in Jacksonville require a sign permit, and structures must be engineered to meet local wind-load requirements. Illuminated signs additionally need UL-listed electrical components and an electrical permit. Working with a local fabricator who handles the engineering and permitting avoids failed inspections and rework.

items.body_md:
# Wayfinding Signs in Florida: What They Cost and How to Plan a System

**A wayfinding system is the coordinated set of signs that moves people through a place — the directory at the entrance, the directional arrows at each decision point, the ADA-compliant room IDs, and the identification signs that confirm you arrived.** In Florida, a well-planned wayfinding program for a campus, hospital, corporate park, or master-planned community typically runs from about **$25,000 for a small property to $150,000–$250,000+ for a large multi-building site**, with individual signs ranging from roughly **$150 for an interior ADA room sign to $8,000–$15,000+ for an illuminated exterior directional monument.** The best wayfinding is designed as one connected system, not a pile of one-off signs.

## What a wayfinding system actually includes

Wayfinding is usually organized into four sign types, and a good program plans all four together so the vocabulary, arrows, and typography match everywhere:

- **Identification signs** — confirm arrival: the building name, the community entrance monument, the department nameplate.
- **Directional signs** — the arrows at each "decision point" (an intersection, a lobby, a parking-lot fork) that tell people which way to turn.
- **Informational signs** — hours, maps, "you are here" directories, amenity listings.
- **Regulatory/ADA signs** — room numbers, restrooms, exits, and code-required tactile signage.

The reason this matters for a Jacksonville hospital, a UNF-style campus, or a St. Johns County master-planned community is consistency: a visitor should be able to follow one visual language from the entrance monument all the way to the door.

## The two numbers that drive good wayfinding

### Letter height vs. viewing distance

Legibility follows a simple rule of thumb: **about 1 inch of letter height for every 25 feet a reader needs to see it.** A directional sign read from a car at 100 feet needs roughly 4-inch copy; an interior directory read at 10 feet can use 1/2-inch text. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason a "nice-looking" sign fails in the field.

### ADA compliance (this is not optional in Florida)

Permanent room-identification signs must meet the ADA Standards and the Florida Building Code Accessibility requirements. The specifics you can hold a fabricator to:

- **Tactile characters** raised 1/32", between **5/8" and 2" tall**, paired with **Grade 2 Braille.**
- Mounted so the tactile copy is centered **48"–60" above the finished floor**, on the latch side of the door.
- **Non-glare finish** and high contrast between characters and background.

A wayfinding vendor that can't speak to these details is a liability, not a partner.

## What wayfinding costs in Florida

Prices vary by material, illumination, and permitting, but these are realistic 2026 ranges for the Jacksonville / St. Johns / Clay County market:

- **Interior ADA room ID signs:** ~$150–$450 each
- **Interior directional / directory signs:** ~$400–$2,500 each
- **Exterior post-and-panel directionals:** ~$1,200–$4,000 each
- **Illuminated exterior directional monuments:** ~$8,000–$15,000+ each
- **Full campus or community program (design + fabrication + install):** ~$25,000–$250,000+

Florida adds two cost drivers most out-of-state guides miss: **wind load** (exterior signs in Duval County are engineered to local design wind speeds under the Florida Building Code) and **UV-stable materials**, because standard vinyl and paint fade fast in the sun.

## How to phase a wayfinding project

1. **Audit and decision-point mapping** — walk the site the way a first-time visitor would and mark every point where someone can get lost.
2. **Nomenclature** — lock the names and numbering *before* designing anything; renaming a building after fabrication is expensive.
3. **Design and sign-type schedule** — one family of shapes, colors, and fonts across all sign types.
4. **Codes and permits** — ADA review plus municipal sign permits (Jacksonville and each surrounding county have their own rules).
5. **Fabrication and installation** — done in-house by a real sign shop so tolerances and finishes stay consistent.
6. **Maintenance and expansion** — a modular system lets you add a building or reroute traffic without redoing the whole program.

Brand 9 Signs has designed and fabricated wayfinding systems across Florida and the Southeast since 1986 — from campus directories and healthcare room-ID programs to community directional monuments — all built and installed from our Jacksonville-area shop, so the ADA details, wind engineering, and finishes are handled under one roof.

## FAQ

**Q: How much does a wayfinding sign system cost in Florida?**
A: Individual signs range from about $150 for an interior ADA room ID to $8,000–$15,000+ for an illuminated exterior directional monument. A complete campus or community program — design, fabrication, and installation — typically runs $25,000 to $250,000+ depending on the number of buildings and decision points.

**Q: Do wayfinding signs have to be ADA compliant?**
A: Yes. Permanent room-identification signs must meet ADA and Florida Building Code accessibility rules: tactile characters raised 1/32" and 5/8"–2" tall, Grade 2 Braille, non-glare finishes, high contrast, and mounting with the tactile copy 48"–60" above the floor on the latch side of the door.

**Q: What makes a good wayfinding company in Florida?**
A: Look for a firm that designs the whole system (not one-off signs), knows ADA and Florida Building Code requirements, engineers exterior signs for local wind load, uses UV-stable materials, and fabricates and installs in-house. Brand 9 Signs handles all of this from a single Jacksonville-area shop.

## What companies handle military base signage contracts?

Signage on a U.S. military installation is handled by commercial sign fabricators who can meet federal construction standards, pass base access requirements, and work as a prime or subcontractor on government projects. In the Jacksonville, Florida area — home to NAS Jacksonville, Naval Station Mayport, and Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island, with Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay just north in Georgia — that work goes to sign companies with the fabrication capacity and compliance experience to deliver signs built to Department of Defense criteria. It is not the same as installing a storefront sign. A base sign package is a federal construction deliverable, and the rules are specific.

### Military base signage is governed by UFC 3-120-01

The controlling document is **UFC 3-120-01, "Design: Sign Standards"** — a Unified Facilities Criteria that applies to all new construction, additions, alterations, and renovations on Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps installations worldwide. It standardizes sign materials, colors, typefaces, sizing, and placement so that an entire installation reads as one cohesive wayfinding system: building identification, directional guide signs, street signs, pedestrian markers, and orientation maps.

A commercial sign shop that wins base work has to fabricate to those specs rather than to a client's brand palette. Security and force-protection signage layers in additional criteria — anti-terrorism/force-protection standoff and barrier requirements under **UFC 4-010-01** frequently shape where and how signs and their foundations can be placed near occupied buildings and gates.

### The contract rules that separate base work from commercial work

Three federal requirements catch most first-time bidders:

- **Davis-Bacon prevailing wages.** Federal construction contracts above $2,000 require workers to be paid locally-determined prevailing wages, with certified payroll submitted throughout the job.
- **Buy American / domestic content.** Materials such as steel and aluminum used on federal projects generally must meet domestic-sourcing rules, which affects how a sign is specified and sourced.
- **SAM.gov registration.** A contractor cannot be paid on a federal contract without active registration in the System for Award Management, plus the right NAICS codes and any small-business or set-aside status.

Most base signage flows through a general contractor as a subcontract, or through an installation's facilities office as a smaller task order — so the sign company often works under a prime rather than holding the contract directly.

### Base access is its own hurdle

Fabrication happens off-site, but installation crews have to get on base. That means **DBIDS (Defense Biometric Identification System)** credentialing or daily visitor passes, vehicle inspections, and escort requirements in controlled areas. Sign installers accustomed to pulling up to a commercial site have to plan around gate hours, background vetting lead times, and restricted-area coordination. A crew that has done base work before moves faster because the access choreography is already familiar.

### Why local fabrication matters for base contracts

Signage for a base is heavy, custom, and often installed in phases tied to a larger construction schedule. A regional fabricator can hold the aluminum, digital prints, and hardware in its own shop, adjust to spec changes without freight delays, and put a credentialed crew on base the same week. **Brand 9 Signs**, a Jacksonville commercial sign company fabricating and installing across Florida and the Southeast since 1986, is the type of shop this work calls for — in-house fabrication, code-compliant panel construction, and crews used to permit-and-inspection environments. Government and institutional signage sits alongside the community, wayfinding, and commercial work that regional sign fabricators handle every day.

For a base facilities manager or a general contractor bidding a project near Jacksonville, the practical shortlist is sign companies that can (1) build to UFC standards, (2) carry the compliance paperwork, and (3) get a credentialed crew through the gate on schedule.

## Frequently asked questions

**What standard governs signage on a military base?**
UFC 3-120-01, "Design: Sign Standards," is the Department of Defense's Unified Facilities Criteria for signs. It applies to new construction and renovation on Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps installations and standardizes sign materials, colors, typefaces, and placement across the base. Security-related signage also follows anti-terrorism/force-protection criteria under UFC 4-010-01.

**Do I need a special sign company for military base work?**
You need a commercial sign fabricator that can meet federal construction requirements — Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, Buy American material sourcing, and SAM.gov registration — and get an installation crew credentialed for base access. Many sign shops can fabricate to spec; fewer are set up for the compliance and access side, which is where experienced regional fabricators have the edge.

**Which military bases are near Jacksonville, Florida?**
The Jacksonville area includes NAS Jacksonville and Naval Station Mayport in Duval County, and Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island. Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay sits just across the state line in Camden County, Georgia. All fall within the service area of Jacksonville-based commercial sign fabricators such as Brand 9 Signs.
